grades.quote: Another is lazy memory allocation, which allows a program to ask for a huge virtual address space, but only to pay the cost of allocating physical memory for the pages the program actually reads and writes. xv6 uses page faults for only one purpose: lazy allocation.
grades.reason: Explains that an access to an unmapped address raises a page fault, that scause/stval report it, and that xv6 uses page faults for lazy allocation (paying only for pages actually touched). It doesn't mention SBRK_LAZY or say the kernel allocates a page on first access.

grades.quote: Xv6 performs a few: mapping the same memory (a trampoline page) in several address spaces, guarding kernel and user stacks with an unmapped page, and allocating user heap memory lazily.
grades.reason: Only briefly lists lazy heap allocation as one of xv6's page-table tricks. It gives no mechanism for sbrk or for what happens on first access.
Real-world discussion of paging, super pages, ASIDs and kernel allocators. It says nothing about sbrk, SBRK_LAZY or lazy allocation on first access.

grades.quote: when an application asks for memory by calling sbrk with the flag SBRK_LAZY, the kernel notes the increase in size, but does not allocate physical memory and does not create PTEs for the new range of virtual addresses. Second, on a page fault on one of those new addresses, the kernel allocates a page of physical memory and maps it into the page table.
grades.reason: Directly answers both parts. With SBRK_LAZY the kernel only records the size increase and creates no PTEs or physical pages, so sbrk succeeds. On the first access a page fault occurs, and the kernel allocates a physical page and maps it.
